6.1.simple: Real spiritual life is not about dropping your responsibilities. Krishna says the true yogi does what needs doing without clinging to the rewards, unlike someone who simply gives up work or rituals.

6.2.simple: Renunciation and yoga are really the same thing: letting go of selfish wanting. You cannot find inner balance while your mind is busy chasing its own plans and cravings.

6.3.simple: When you are starting out, doing your work well is the path that trains you. Once you reach inner steadiness, calm and stillness help you stay there.

6.4.simple: You have reached yoga when you are no longer hooked by pleasures or by your actions and their results, and you have let go of the endless 'I want' plans in your head.

6.5.simple: You are the one who lifts yourself up. Your own mind can be your best friend or your worst enemy, so treat yourself as someone worth raising, not pulling down.

6.6.simple: When you have learned to guide your own mind, it becomes your ally. When it runs wild, it works against you as if it were an outside enemy.

6.7.simple: A person who has mastered themselves stays calm and settled whether it is hot or cold, pleasant or painful, and whether they are praised or insulted.

6.8.simple: Someone content with real understanding, and in charge of their senses, looks at a lump of clay, a stone and a bar of gold with the same calm eye. Things lose their power to unsettle them.

6.9.simple: The person who truly stands out holds the same goodwill toward everyone: friends, rivals, strangers, family, the kind and the unkind. A fair heart is a sign of real growth.

6.10.simple: To steady the mind, Krishna suggests regular time alone in a quiet place, with body and mind settled and free from restless craving and grasping.

6.11.simple: Meditation starts practically: find a clean, quiet spot and a steady seat, neither too high nor too low. In Krishna's time this meant layers of grass, skin and cloth.

6.12.simple: Sitting there, gather your attention to one point and let your thoughts and senses settle. The purpose of the practice is to clear and purify your inner life.

6.13.simple: Keep your body, head and neck upright and still, and let your gaze rest softly, as if toward the tip of your nose, instead of glancing around. A steady body helps a steady mind.

6.14.simple: Sit calm and unafraid, keeping a disciplined, self-restrained way of life (brahmacharya), with your mind gathered and resting on Krishna as your highest aim.

6.15.simple: Practicing this way again and again, with a balanced and gathered mind, the yogi reaches a deep peace that rests in Krishna and leads to freedom (liberation).

6.16.simple: Extremes get in the way. Meditation does not work well for someone who overeats or starves, or who oversleeps or hardly sleeps. The body needs care, not punishment.

6.17.simple: Moderation in food, play, work, sleep and waking is what lets yoga ease suffering. A balanced daily routine is itself a spiritual practice.

6.18.simple: A person is truly 'united' in yoga when their trained mind rests in the deeper Self and no longer craves the things of the senses.

6.19.simple: A well-trained mind is like a lamp in a place with no wind: its flame does not flicker. That steady, quiet glow is the picture of a mind settled in meditation.

6.20.simple: As practice calms the mind, it grows quiet, and you begin to see your true Self by your own inner light, finding contentment within instead of outside.

6.21.simple: In that state there is a deep joy beyond the senses, known by a clear and pure understanding. Once settled there, a person does not drift away from what is real.

6.22.simple: Having found this inner joy, you see no gain greater than it, and even heavy sorrow cannot shake you. It is a shelter that holds when life is hard.

6.23.simple: Yoga means unhooking from suffering. Krishna asks us to practice it with determination and without losing heart, even when progress seems slow.

6.24.simple: Let go of the cravings our imagination keeps cooking up, and use the mind to gently rein in the senses from every side.

6.25.simple: Go step by step. With patient, steady understanding, settle the mind in the Self and stop feeding other thoughts. Slow progress is still real progress.

6.26.simple: Whenever the restless mind wanders, for whatever reason, simply bring it back. This gentle returning, over and over, is the heart of meditation.

6.27.simple: Deep joy comes to the meditator whose mind is calm, whose passions have quieted, who is free from wrongdoing and becomes one with Brahman (the infinite reality).

6.28.simple: By practicing steadily like this, the yogi is cleansed of past wrongs and easily enjoys the boundless happiness of touching Brahman (the infinite reality).

6.29.simple: A mind made steady by yoga sees the same Self in every being, and every being in that Self. It looks on everyone with an equal, fair eye.

6.30.simple: Whoever sees Krishna everywhere, and everything in Krishna, is never lost to Krishna, and Krishna is never lost to them. It is a promise of a bond that does not break.

6.31.simple: A person rooted in this sense of oneness, who honors Krishna present in all beings, lives in Krishna, whatever their outer way of life looks like.

6.32.simple: The highest yogi feels others' joy and pain as their own, using their own heart as the measure. Compassion is a sign of real spiritual maturity.

6.33.simple: Arjuna is honest: this balanced state sounds wonderful, but his mind feels too restless to hold it steadily. It is a doubt almost everyone has felt.

6.34.simple: Arjuna calls the mind restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna does not scold him for saying so.

6.35.simple: Krishna agrees the mind is hard to control, but says it can be trained through two things: steady practice and letting go of attachment (detachment).

6.36.simple: Without self-discipline this yoga is hard to reach, but anyone who keeps trying with the right methods can get there.

6.37.simple: Arjuna asks a tender question: what happens to someone with sincere faith who tries, but whose mind slips off the path before reaching the goal?

6.38.simple: He worries such a person might lose both worldly success and spiritual progress, drifting like a broken cloud with nothing to hold on to.

6.39.simple: Arjuna asks Krishna to clear this doubt completely, trusting that no one else can answer it as well as he can.

6.40.simple: Krishna's answer is deeply reassuring: no one who does good ever comes to a bad end, in this world or the next. Sincere effort is never wasted.

6.41.simple: The one who strays from yoga first enjoys the worlds of good people for a long time, then is born into a pure and prosperous family where growth is easier.

6.42.simple: Or they may be born into a family of wise yogis, a rare and precious birth that gives them a strong start.

6.43.simple: There, the understanding they gained before comes back to them, and they strive even harder for the goal. Progress picks up where it left off.

6.44.simple: Their earlier practice carries them forward almost on its own. Even someone who simply wants to know yoga goes beyond mere ritual and book learning.

6.45.simple: By striving sincerely and being purified little by little over many lives, the yogi finally reaches the highest goal. Growth adds up over time.

6.46.simple: Krishna rates the yogi above those who only practice hardship, those who only study, and those who only perform rituals or works, and urges Arjuna to be a yogi.

6.47.simple: Of all yogis, Krishna holds dearest the one who, full of faith and with a heart absorbed in him, lovingly worships him. Devotion crowns the practice.

lessons.title: Be your own best friend
lessons.teaching: Spiritual life is not about escaping your duties; it is doing what needs doing without clinging to rewards. No one else can lift you up for you. Your own mind can become your best friend or your harshest enemy, and you get to choose which.
lessons.keyIdea: Your own mind can be your best friend or your worst enemy.

apply.scenario: You failed an important exam, and your inner voice keeps saying 'you're hopeless, why bother?' A friend suggests you just drop the course.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Drop the course quietly so you never have to feel this bad again.
Wait for a teacher or parent to step in and tell you what to do next.
Speak to yourself like a good friend would: admit the setback, then make a small plan to lift yourself up.
Keep replaying the failure until you feel bad enough to finally change.
apply.why: In 6.5 Krishna says we should raise ourselves by our own effort and never drag ourselves down, because the self can be our friend or our enemy.

lessons.reflect: When things go wrong, does your inner voice sound more like a friend or a critic?
lessons.practice: Notice one harsh thought about yourself today and rewrite it the way a kind friend would say it.

lessons.title: Stay steady through praise and blame
lessons.teaching: When you learn to guide your mind, it becomes your ally. A settled person stays balanced in heat or cold, pleasure or pain, honor or insult, and offers the same goodwill to everyone. Quiet time alone helps build this steadiness.
lessons.keyIdea: Stay the same person whether you are praised or criticized.

apply.scenario: On Monday your manager praised you in a meeting; on Thursday she criticized your report in front of the team. You feel like a hero one day and a failure the next.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Take the feedback calmly, learn what is useful, and let neither the praise nor the criticism define you.
Bring up Monday's praise to remind everyone that you are actually good at this.
Stop sharing your work in meetings so you can't be criticized in public again.
Decide your manager dislikes you and stay cool and distant with her from now on.
apply.why: In 6.7 Krishna describes the self-mastered person as balanced in pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor.

lessons.reflect: Whose approval moves your mood the most, and what would it feel like to depend on it a little less?
lessons.practice: Spend five quiet minutes alone today, phone away, simply noticing your breath.

lessons.title: Set up a simple meditation habit
lessons.teaching: Krishna gives down-to-earth instructions for meditation: a clean, quiet spot, a steady seat, an upright body and a gathered mind. He also warns against extremes. Eating or sleeping too much or too little makes practice harder, not holier.
lessons.keyIdea: A clean spot, a steady seat, an upright spine, a gathered mind.

apply.scenario: You want to start meditating. A friend says the 'serious' way is to skip meals and cut your sleep to four hours so your mind gets sharper.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Follow your friend's plan, since harder must mean more spiritual.
Meditate lying in bed with your phone nearby so it feels relaxed and easy.
Wait until you can manage a silent retreat before starting at all.
Choose a clean, quiet corner, sit upright on a steady seat, and keep your normal meals and sleep.
apply.why: In 6.11-6.13 Krishna describes a clean spot, a steady seat and an upright posture, and in 6.16 he says yoga is not for those who eat or sleep too much or too little.

lessons.reflect: What small corner or time of day could become your quiet place?
lessons.practice: Sit upright for three minutes in a clean, quiet spot and rest your attention gently on your breath.

lessons.title: A lamp where no wind blows
lessons.teaching: Moderation in food, rest, work and sleep is what allows practice to ease suffering. A settled mind is like a lamp in a windless place: its flame stays still. In that stillness you find a deep joy that does not depend on outside things.
lessons.keyIdea: A balanced life lets the mind glow like a lamp without wind.

apply.scenario: You are building a side business and have been working until 2 a.m., skipping meals, then crashing all weekend. You feel anxious and scattered.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Push even harder for a few months; balance can come after you succeed.
Set regular times for meals, work, a short break and sleep so your mind can settle.
Give up the business, since it is clearly too stressful for you.
Rely on energy drinks during the week and sleep all weekend to recover.
apply.why: In 6.17 Krishna says yoga removes suffering for one who is moderate in eating, recreation, work, sleep and waking.

lessons.reflect: Where in your daily routine are you swinging between too much and too little?
lessons.practice: Pick one fixed bedtime for tonight and keep it.

lessons.title: Gently bring the mind back
lessons.teaching: Yoga is the art of unhooking from suffering, practiced with determination and without losing heart. Progress comes little by little. Whenever the mind wanders, for any reason, you simply bring it back, again and again.
lessons.keyIdea: Every time you bring the wandering mind back, you are doing it right.

apply.scenario: You sit for ten quiet minutes before bed, but your mind keeps jumping to tomorrow's job interview and you start to feel you are bad at this.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Give up; some people's minds just aren't made for quiet sitting.
Force your mind to go blank and get annoyed each time a thought appears.
Each time you notice the mind has wandered, gently bring it back and keep going, little by little.
Switch to a different technique every night until one feels effortless.
apply.why: In 6.26 Krishna says that whenever the restless mind wanders, we should simply bring it back, and 6.25 adds that steadiness comes little by little.

lessons.reflect: How do you usually speak to yourself when your attention slips?
lessons.practice: Count ten breaths; each time you lose count, smile and start again at one.

lessons.title: See yourself in everyone
lessons.teaching: As the mind grows calm, a deep joy arises, and with it a new way of seeing: the same Self lives in every being. Whoever sees Krishna everywhere is never apart from him, whatever their outer life looks like.
lessons.keyIdea: The same Self lives in every being, even the ones you find difficult.

apply.scenario: A cousin you have always found annoying is staying with your family for a week, and you are tempted to hide in your room the whole time.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Stay polite but distant; you don't have to connect with everyone.
Complain to your parents until they shorten the visit.
Spend time together but quietly count the hours until they leave.
Look for the same hopes, fears and goodness in them that you have, and spend some real time together.
apply.why: In 6.29 Krishna says a person steadied by yoga sees the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, looking on everyone with an equal eye.

lessons.reflect: Who in your life is hardest to see as 'like you', and what might you have in common?
lessons.practice: Today, silently wish one person you find difficult: 'May you be well.'

lessons.title: The restless mind can be trained
lessons.teaching: The highest yogi feels others' joy and pain as their own. Arjuna honestly admits his mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Krishna agrees, but says practice and letting go can train it. With the right methods, steady effort works.
lessons.keyIdea: The mind is restless like the wind, yet practice and letting go steady it.

apply.scenario: You reach for your phone every few minutes while working, and you have started to believe you are just 'a distracted person' who can't change.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Accept it; some minds are simply wired to be scattered.
Admit it's hard, then practice short daily focus sessions and gently loosen your pull toward the phone.
Delete every app in one dramatic move and hope your willpower holds.
Wait until you feel naturally motivated before trying to focus again.
apply.why: In 6.35 Krishna agrees the mind is restless and hard to control, but says it can be trained through steady practice and detachment.

lessons.reflect: What habit of mind have you assumed you can never change?
lessons.practice: Put your phone in another room for one 25-minute focus session today.

lessons.title: Sincere effort is never wasted
lessons.teaching: Arjuna fears that someone who tries and falls short loses everything. Krishna reassures him warmly: no one who does good ever comes to a bad end. Even unfinished effort carries forward and opens better chances to grow.
lessons.keyIdea: No one who does good ever comes to a bad end.

apply.scenario: You spent two years training for a career that didn't work out. Now you feel those years were wasted and that you have fallen behind everyone.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Recognize that the effort, skills and character you built still count, and carry them into what comes next.
Conclude it was a mistake to try and play it safe from now on.
Leave those two years off your resume and avoid mentioning them to friends.
Work twice as hard to make up for the 'lost' time as quickly as possible.
apply.why: In 6.40 Krishna tells Arjuna that one who does good never comes to grief, in this world or the next.

lessons.reflect: What past effort that 'didn't work out' has quietly shaped who you are now?
lessons.practice: Write down three things you gained from an effort you once thought was a failure.

lessons.title: Keep going; growth adds up
lessons.teaching: Good practice is never lost: it returns and carries you forward, sometimes almost on its own. Growth builds over time. Krishna urges Arjuna to be a yogi and says the dearest is one who practices with faith and a loving heart.
lessons.keyIdea: Every sincere step you take keeps carrying you forward.

apply.scenario: You played the guitar every day as a teenager but stopped for years. Picking it up again, you wonder whether it is pointless to start over.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Don't bother; you've lost too much ground to ever catch up.
Only restart if you can practice three hours a day like you used to.
Start again with heart; your earlier practice will come back faster than you expect.
Read about guitar technique online instead of actually playing.
apply.why: In 6.43-6.44 Krishna says the understanding gained before comes back, and earlier practice carries a person forward almost by itself.

lessons.reflect: What practice in your life is waiting for you to come back to it?
lessons.practice: Spend ten minutes today on one good practice you have let slip.
